```{R}
#| label: load-pkg-data
#| message: false

install.packages("kableExtra")
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(patchwork)

ai_salary_majors <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-10-20/ai_salary_majors.csv')
major_occupations <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-10-20/major_occupations.csv')
```

```{R}
glimpse(ai_salary_majors)
```

```{R}
#| label: distribution-visualization

ggplot(ai_salary_majors, aes(x = ai_exposure)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of AI exposure across majors",
    x = "AI exposure (how much a major’s typical jobs rely on abilities related 
    to common AI applications)",
    y = "Number of majors"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(ai_salary_majors, aes(x = median_starting_salary)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5000, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(ai_salary_majors$median_starting_salary),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of median starting salary across majors",
    x = "Median salary one year after graduation",
    y = "Number of majors"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
```{R}
#| label: initial-exploration-exposure-salary
#| fig-cap: "AI exposure vs. median starting salary for 285 majors"

ggplot(ai_salary_majors, aes(x = ai_exposure, y = median_starting_salary)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "AI exposure and starting salary across majors",
    x = "AI exposure (0 = average occupation; higher = more exposed)",
    y = "Median starting salary"
  ) 
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
Across 285 majors, overall AI exposure has essentially no linear relationship 
with median starting salary. Highly exposed and less exposed majors both span a 
wide range of pay, but the number of majors that have high exposure to AI is
significantly higher than the number of majors that do not. 
:::
```{R}
#| label: major-regrouping
ai_salary_majors <- ai_salary_majors |>
  mutate(
    field_group = fct_collapse(
      broad_field_short,
      "Engineering & architecture" = c("Engineering", "Engineering Tech", "Architecture"),
      "Computing & math" = c("Computer Science", "Mathematics & Statistics"),
      "Natural sciences & agriculture" = c("Biological Sciences", "Physical Sciences", "Science Tech",
                                           "Agriculture", "Natural Resources"),
      "Health" = c("Health Professions"),
      "Business, law & public service" = c("Business", "Legal", "Public Administration", "Homeland Security"),
      "Social sciences & education" = c("Social Sciences", "Psychology", "Education", "Family & Consumer Sci",
                                        "Parks & Recreation", "Area & Ethnic Studies", "Library Science"),
      "Humanities, arts & communication" = c("English", "Foreign Languages", "History", "Philosophy & Religion",
                                             "Theology & Religion", "Visual & Performing Arts",
                                             "Communication", "Communications Tech"),
      "Trades & transportation" = c("Construction Trades", "Mechanic & Repair Tech", "Precision Production",
                                    "Transportation", "Culinary & Personal Svc", "Military Tech"),
      "Interdisciplinary" = c("Interdisciplinary")
    ),
    field_group = fct_relevel(field_group, "Humanities, arts & communication")
  )
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
For graphing, 37 facet panels was unreadable, and many families have only 1–4 
majors, which is too few to show a trend. So for the plots only, I combined the 
CIP families into 9 broader groups based on the kind of work graduates 
of each family typically dodo. Fields in the same group should look similar 
on the plot
:::

```{R}
#| label: exposure-salary-by-group
#| fig-cap: "AI exposure vs. median starting salary within each field group"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
ggplot(ai_salary_majors, aes(x = ai_exposure, y = median_starting_salary)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ field_group, ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"))+
  labs(
    title = "AI exposure vs. starting salary, by field group",
    x = "AI exposure",
    y = "Median starting salary"
  ) 
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
For almost all groups, the relationship between AI exposure and starting salary 
is weak. Most lines are nearly flat or slightly positive, and the points 
scatter widely around them. However, it is interesting to note that the
engineering and architecture group appears to have the highest salary level 
out of all groups. 
:::

```{R}
r_lang_img <- cor(ai_salary_majors$ai_exposure_language, 
                  ai_salary_majors$ai_exposure_image)

ggplot(ai_salary_majors, aes(x = ai_exposure_language, y = ai_exposure_image)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
  geom_point(aes(color = field_group), alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Language and image AI exposure correlation",
    subtitle = paste0("r = ", round(r_lang_img, 2)),
    x = "AI Language exposure",
    y = "AI Image exposure",
    color = "Major Employment Group"
  )
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
The correlation between AI language exposure and AI image exposure is only 0.48,
indicating that some majors are exposed to one kind significantly more than the
other. As can be seen from the graph, the humanities, arts, and communication
group and the social sciences and education group lean towards language 
exposure, while the engineering and architecture group lean towards image 
exposure. 
:::

```{R}
#| label: numeric-edas

eda_lang <- ggplot(ai_salary_majors, aes(x = ai_exposure_language, y = median_starting_salary)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(title = "Language exposure", x = "Language exposure", y = "Median starting salary") +
  theme_minimal()

eda_img <- ggplot(ai_salary_majors, aes(x = ai_exposure_image, y = median_starting_salary)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(title = "Image exposure", x = "Image exposure", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

eda_lang + eda_img
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
Both exposure predictors look roughly linear with salary, so they don't need 
transforming. Log transformation do not make sense since they include negative 
values. Salary is right-skewed, so a log transform of salary might be needed.
:::

```{R}
#| label: salary-by-field-eda
#| fig-cap: "Median starting salary by CIP family, ordered by median salary"

ai_salary_majors |>
  mutate(broad_field_short = fct_reorder(broad_field_short, 
                                         median_starting_salary)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = median_starting_salary, y = broad_field_short)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, 
                                                   suffix = "k")) +
  labs(x = "Median starting salary", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
Median starting salary varies widely across CIP families, from about 19k to 73k, 
so CIP field is likely an important predictor.
:::

```{R}
#| fig-cap: "Base model with no transformation"

base_model <- lm(median_starting_salary ~ ai_exposure_language + 
                   ai_exposure_image + broad_field_short,
                data = ai_salary_majors)

tidy(base_model) |>
  kable(digits = 3) 
```

```{R}
#| fig-cap: "The distribution of residuals is approximately normal"
augment_base_model <- augment(base_model)

ggplot(augment_base_model, aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(x = "Residuals",
       y = "Count",
       title = "Distribution of Residuals")
```
```{R}
#| fig-cap: "Vertical spread does not appear to be constant"
ggplot(augment_base_model, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Fitted Values",
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values")
```

```{R}
#| fig-cap: "Vertical spread does not appear to be constant "
ggplot(augment_base_model, aes(x = ai_exposure_language, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Language Exposure",
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs. Language Exposure")

ggplot(augment_base_model, aes(x = ai_exposure_image, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Image Exposure",
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs. Image Exposure")
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
Since the vertical spread for all of the residual plots appear to be
non-constant, a log transformation on response should be considered
:::

```{R}
log_fit <- lm(log(median_starting_salary) ~ ai_exposure_language + 
                ai_exposure_image + broad_field_short, data = ai_salary_majors)

tidy(log_fit) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{R}
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of residuals appear approximately normal"
augment_log_fit <- augment(log_fit)

ggplot(augment_log_fit, aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(x = "Residuals",
       y = "Count",
       title = "Distribution of Residuals (Log Model)")

ggplot(augment_log_fit, aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
       y = "Sample Quantiles",
       title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals (Log Model)")
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
The normal Q-Q plot shows that the residuals follow the line closely in the 
middle but bend away at both ends, indicating heavier tails than a normal 
distribution. However, as the bends appear roughly symmetric and given that 
there are 285 observations, normality can be assumed. 
:::
```{R}
ggplot(augment_log_fit, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Fitted Values (log salary)",
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values (Log Model)")
```

```{R}
ggplot(augment_log_fit, aes(x = ai_exposure_language, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Language Exposure",
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs. Language Exposure (Log Model)")

ggplot(augment_log_fit, aes(x = ai_exposure_image, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Image Exposure",
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs. Image Exposure (Log Model)")
```
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
The vertical spread of residuals is more even compared to the base model, as the 
residuals no longer fan out at high fitted values. 
However, residuals are still tightly clustered at low fitted values and most
spread out in the middle range, so the equal variance condition is only partly 
met. Since we've only learned log transformation and I've spent way too long
on this project already, I will just take this model (can't log the predictor 
since they have negative values).
:::
